summary.game: 600 rounds of rock-paper-scissors, Claude choosing every move one round at a time, against an LSTM that retrains after each round on the player's full move history and plays the counter to its prediction.
summary.verdict: Claude was smarter at understanding the game; the LSTM was better at the one thing this game rewards over a long match: finding patterns in the opponent's moves. After round ~120 the match was a draw.
where_claude_was_ahead: Rounds 8-77 went 35-15: Claude understood the mechanics (it predicts my move and counters it; I lose only when it guesses my exact move; it learns slowly at first) while the AI had no idea what Claude was doing.

Diagnosis: Claude found that its own formula randomizer had a hidden rock-paper-scissors cycle, discovered that PowerShell's Get-Random was not independent across processes, measured which rules actually worked, and dropped the ones that didn't. The LSTM cannot reason about why it wins or loses.
where_lstm_was_ahead: Every rule Claude used was a function of its own move history, and the LSTM learned each one: counter-cycles, switching after a win, reactions to its streaks. Claude usually noticed only after losing several rounds.

The LSTM exploited the faulty coin flip (rock after rock 52% of the time) long before Claude found it at round 444. Detecting statistical regularities is exactly what it is built for, and it never tires.
summary.why_it_ended_close: Once Claude switched to a cryptographic random generator, neither side had anything to exploit. In rock-paper-scissors, random play cannot be beaten but also cannot win on average. The final margin is the early lead minus the Get-Random losses, plus variance (the last 100 pure-random rounds went 34-41).
caveats: Very different opponents: the LSTM is a tiny network (~1-2k parameters) that does one thing, predict the next move from the last 6; Claude is a general model reasoning deliberately about the game.

Asymmetric information: Claude saw the AI's prediction after each round, while the LSTM learned only from Claude's moves. Claude had more information; the LSTM had more patience and learned automatically every round.
summary.takeaway: Understanding the game gave an early edge. The skill that decided the long match was avoiding patterns of your own, and Claude kept failing at that until it switched to true randomness.

opponent: LSTM(16) -> dense(3, softmax), WINDOW=6, Adam, categoricalCrossentropy, 20 epochs per round on full history, TF.js 4.22 CPU (sim/play.js)
strategy_summary: Rounds 1-7: AI plays randomly until it has data; played only rock to plant a habit.

Rounds 8-77: read the AI. Key rule: I lose only when it predicts my exact move, so I mostly played the move it gave the lowest probability, hedged between its two likely predictions, and exploited its slow early learning. Strong early edge that faded as the LSTM learned my reasoning habits (it picked up my counter-cycles and my switch-after-win habit).

Rounds 78-172: tried to become unpredictable with a formula pseudo-random choice (from the AI's displayed percentages plus the round number) and a sliding-window expected-value rule. Both measured ~0 edge; the formula also degenerated into a learnable rock-paper-scissors cycle when the AI's probabilities were extreme.

Rounds 173-444: coin flips via PowerShell Get-Random plus streak overrides (when the AI predicted the same move 3+ rounds in a row, play the move that beats its reply). The override was the one reliably positive rule for a long time. Lost ground here: analysis at round 444 showed Get-Random was not independent across separate processes (rock followed rock 52% of the time), a pattern the LSTM exploited.

Rounds 445-600: switched to the OS cryptographic RNG. At round 500, analysis showed the AI's own prediction sequence had become near-uniform (same/beats/loses-to previous: 33.5/36/30.5%), so streak overrides no longer had an edge; played pure crypto-random (the Nash equilibrium) for the last 100 rounds.

Takeaway: any decision rule that is a function of my own move history eventually becomes learnable by an online-trained sequence model; exploitation works only until it adapts, and only true randomness is safe. The lead was built almost entirely in the first ~120 rounds.
